name: Jaw expansion via MSE / SARPE
lead: SARPE (surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion) and MSE or MARPE (miniscrew- or microimplant-assisted rapid palatal expansion) are ways of widening the upper jaw in adults whose midpalatal suture has fused. In looksmaxxing communities people discuss them as a route to a broader upper jaw, a wider smile arch and more room for the teeth, often alongside braces or bimaxillary surgery, with some hoping for changes in midface width as well.[1][15][17]

In SARPE an oral and maxillofacial surgeon cuts the midpalatal suture, and an orthodontist then activates an expander cemented to the upper teeth.[1][18] MARPE anchors the expander to the palatal bone with mini-implants so that expansion can be attempted without cutting the bone, though Wikipedia notes that most adults, especially men, may still need a surgical assist for consistent results.[1] A 2008 literature review described SARPE as having gradually gained popularity for adults with maxillary transverse deficiency.[2]

Published research is mostly about dental and skeletal measurements: how many millimetres of expansion occur, how much of it relapses, and what complications arise. Studies report that roughly a quarter to a third of dental expansion is lost after treatment, that skeletal expansion is modest but stable, and that major complications are uncommon.[3][8][7][6] The studies measure bite and arch width rather than facial appearance.

paras: Palatal expansion widens the upper jaw so the upper and lower teeth fit together. Wikipedia describes it as most common between about ages 8 and 18, when the suture can still be separated by orthopaedic force; in older patients the change is increasingly dental, with teeth tipping outward rather than bone widening.[1] It is commonly used to correct posterior crossbite, relieve upper-arch crowding and, in some patients with a narrow palate, to widen the airway.[1][18]

For mature palates there are two main routes. SARPE combines surgery with an orthodontic expander: under anaesthesia the surgeon releases the fused bone, often at the midpalatal suture and sometimes the pterygomaxillary junction, and the patient or orthodontist then turns the expander over the following weeks.[1][18] MARPE (also marketed or discussed as MSE) uses mini-implants placed in the palatal vault so the force acts on bone instead of only on the teeth; Wikipedia describes it as less invasive than SARPE and producing more skeletal than dentoalveolar expansion.[1] A 2017 paper described the MARPE technique developed by Dr Won Moon and colleagues at UCLA and concluded that it could be an alternative to SARPE in most non-growing patients with maxillary transverse deficiency.[5]

Expansion of the palate dates to the nineteenth century. Wikipedia reports that Emerson Angell published the first paper on palatal expansion in 1860, describing a screw used in a 14-year-old girl, and that the Haas expander was reintroduced in the United States in 1956 and the tooth-borne Hyrax appliance in 1968.[1] For adults, the SARPE article credits Brown with first describing the surgical technique in 1938, Kole with discussing corticotomy for adult maxillary constriction in 1959, and Steinhauser with the segmental split technique in 1972.[18] These dates are as given by Wikipedia.

Mini-implant-anchored expanders are a more recent development, described in the orthodontic literature in the 2010s as a way to treat grown patients without osteotomies.[5] The 2008 review noted SARPE had gradually gained popularity in the preceding years for adults.[2]

Studies measure two things: how far the teeth move apart (dental expansion) and how far the bone itself widens (skeletal expansion). A prospective study of 20 adults found a mean maximum expansion at the first molar of 7.48 mm, with 30 percent of dental expansion lost during post-surgical orthodontics; skeletal expansion averaged 3.49 mm and was stable, so about 67 percent of the net expansion was skeletal. The authors advised clinicians to expect loss of about a third of dental expansion.[9] A follow-up of 38 patients reported a mean maximum molar expansion of 7.60 mm and mean relapse of 1.83 mm (24 percent), concluding that skeletal changes were modest but stable and that dental relapse was mostly lingual movement of the back teeth.[3]

An earlier longitudinal study of 14 patients aged 18 to 41 found larger transverse increases at the first molars (8.7 mm) and premolars than at the canines (5.2 mm) and second molars (5.5 mm), with mean total dental relapse of 28 percent. Skeletal change measured on radiographs was about 1.3 mm near the osteotomy site, and the authors described the skeletal effect as mainly a lateral rotation of the two maxillary halves with little translation.[8] Taken together, these papers show a range of skeletal contribution depending on how it is measured.

A comparison of 10 SARPE patients and 10 who had segmental Le Fort I bipartition found average gains of 8.5 mm at the intercanine and 7 mm at the intermolar width after SARPE, with 28 and 36 percent relapse at two years; the Le Fort I group gained less but relapsed 25 and 20 percent.[10] The authors concluded the segmental osteotomy was more stable, especially at the molars.

A systematic review of complications of surgically assisted maxillary expansion pooled 12 articles covering 851 patients and found 187 reported complications (21.97 percent). The most common minor ones were epistaxis (2.47 percent) and postoperative pain (2.00 percent), with asymmetric or inadequate expansion at 4.47 percent; the authors reported that omitting pterygomaxillary disjunction was associated with more minor complications and that slow distraction patterns were associated with more orthodontic complications, and concluded that complications are mostly minor with low occurrence rates.[7]

A retrospective cohort of 120 patients at one US medical centre (median age 29.5) found 41 had at least one complication; asymmetric or inadequate expansion was the most frequent surgical complication (13.3 percent) and gingival recession (8.3 percent) the most common dental one. Two patients developed severe periodontal bone defects leading to loss of central incisors after eccentric interdental osteotomies and infections; the authors called major complications rare.[6]

A prospective study of 376 SARPEs and 750 Le Fort I procedures reported no life-threatening haemorrhage after SARPE, one non-life-threatening epistaxis requiring packing under general anaesthesia, and two life-threatening bleeds after Le Fort I.[4] A study of periodontal effects in 14 patients with a mean expansion of 9.82 mm found little clinical harm to the gums at 6 months but significant radiographic thinning of buccal bone and reduction of buccal crest level, which the authors said could eventually matter clinically.[11] Wikipedia also lists speech difficulty, extra saliva, pain, tongue sores and a temporary gap between the front teeth as effects of expanders generally.[1]

Published studies include prospective series of 14, 20 and 38 adults on expansion and relapse,[3][8][9] comparisons with segmental Le Fort I osteotomy,[10] complication cohorts and reviews,[2][6][7] and a description of the MARPE technique with a case report.[5] These studies report on bite, arch width, airway and periodontal outcomes and do not assess facial appearance or cheek contour.

Registered trials include a randomised comparison of 2- versus 3-segment SARPE (n=50, started 2013),[12] an observational comparison of tooth-borne, bone-borne and hybrid distraction after SARPE (n=90, started 2021),[13] and an investigation of skeletally anchored maxillary expansion (n=90, started 2025).[14]

On looksmax.org, members compare SARPE with MSE, ask which gives more expansion, and discuss pairing expansion with braces, jaw surgery or other procedures. Threads ask whether expansion changes hollow cheeks or midface width and relay patients' accounts of how much they expanded.[15][16][17] Orthodontists and surgeons in the published literature describe the indication as a transverse deficiency of the bite, not cosmetic width, so the forum discussion extends the treatment to an appearance goal that the studies have not measured.[2][5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org users compare SARPE and MSE and combine them with braces and jaw surgery, discussing expansion amounts and effects on cheek hollows [15][16][17].

claims.claim: SARPE can expand more than MSE, around 15 mm versus 12 mm.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster cited an account from a patient who said she expanded 15 mm with SARPE [16].
claims.experts: Published work describes variable expansion and relapse after SARPE; no source here supports specific millimetre claims [2][3].

claims.claim: Palatal expansion can change midface width and hollow cheeks.
claims.believers: Forum users ask whether SARPE or MSE affects hollow cheeks and discuss expansion as a way to widen the midface [17][16].
claims.experts: Clinical literature focuses on dental and skeletal transverse changes and stability, not cheek appearance [3][9].

card.summary: Surgical or mini-implant jaw widening for adults; real orthodontic procedures with documented complications, discussed in forums as a facial-width tool.
card.note: Surgery with documented complications including rare haemorrhage.

quick.overview:
SARPE and MSE are ways to widen the upper jaw in adults. SARPE uses surgery to free the palate; MSE uses mini-implants to anchor an expander.

They are established orthodontic treatments for transverse deficiency, and forums discuss them for appearance.
quick.mechanism: An expander applies force across the midpalatal suture, after surgical release in SARPE or via bone anchors in MSE/MARPE [1].
quick.risks: Reported problems include pain, relapse, periodontal effects and rare life-threatening haemorrhage [1][4][7].

angle.text: SARPE and MARPE are established treatments for a narrow upper jaw, correcting crossbite and crowding. Looksmaxxing members discuss them for the broader dental arch and the possible effect on midface width and cheek contour; the published studies measure arch width and stability rather than facial appearance.
